newsitem.title: FRANCE: France displays tight grip on far-flung holdings.
newsitem.headline: France displays tight grip on far-flung holdings.

text.p: The presence on Saturday of French troops on the streets of the Central African Republic and gendarmes in French Guiana shows that Paris still has a deep hold on its far-flung holdings and former colonies.

When an army rebellion occurred on Saturday in Bangui, capital of the Central African Republic, French troops stationed nearby were quickly on the spot, patrolling near the presidential palace in a high-profile effort to keep things calm.
It was the third time since September 1995 that French soldiers had moved in to help prop up the shaky rule of President Ange-Felix Patasse
Similarly, when riots broke out this week in Cayenne, the capital of French Guiana in northern South America, Paris flew in 500 riot police from mainland France to restore order.
French Guiana has been in French hands since the 17th century and is the only non-independent territory remaining on the continent.

It is one of four overseas French departments, giving it equal status, administratively speaking, with mainland France. The others are all islands -- Guadeloupe and Martinique in the Caribbean and Reunion in the Indian Ocean.
Paris pours money into French Guiana, as it does into its former colonies, in the form of economic and military aid.
When Patasse could not pay his army, for example, Paris simply paid the soldiers with French taxpayer funds.

The French public, however, generally views such ties as a measure of Paris's global influence rather than as a burden. The spread of French culture, language and power are praised as a source of pride rather than attacked as a waste of money.

France's possessiveness about its former colonial empire was on display last month when a cabinet minister sparked a row with Washington by openly criticising a trip to Africa by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher.

Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain said Christopher's trip fell just before U.S. elections and President Bill Clinton, seeking a new mandate, had never visited Africa during his first four years in office.

U.S. officials accused France of being upset because it viewed Christopher's trip as trespassing on French turf. After Washington complained, Godfrain issued a statement saying he "rejoiced" at Christopher's trip.
In another intervention in a far-flung corner of the globe, France pledged to pour aid into French Polynesia after deciding to dismantle its South Pacific nuclear testing sites.
France's decision last year to conduct a final series of tests on its Mururoa and Fangataufa atolls in the South Pacific had sparked bloody riots in Tahiti by Polynesian separatists.
Other high-profile French actions included a mission to the Comoros islands last year following a coup d'etat there by French soldier of fortune Bob Denard.
Paris sent troops to the tiny Indian Ocean archipelago, a former French colony, to arrest Denard and his band of white mercenaries after they overthrew president Mohamed Said Djohar.
France did not return Djohar to power, however, and Denard asserted that France had approved of his intervention.
